text: Philology is not usually where a comedy goes looking for a father and a son at war. In Jerusalem, Eliezer and Uriel Shkolnik both give their lives to the study of the Jewish scriptures: the father exacting, unhurried and unrewarded; the son admired and quoted by colleagues who barely register the older man's work. Then the telephone rings, and the arrangement that let those two sit at the same table stops holding. Joseph Cedar keeps the register dry, and presses instead on how small a scholar's grievance looks from outside the field and how total it feels within it. Academic standing is this family's only currency, so a change in it is a change in who each man is at dinner. Israel sent the film to the Academy Awards, a strange errand for a story about work nobody reads.

A prosecutor in the late 1950s decides that the fastest route to a German courtroom runs through a foreign intelligence service. West Germany is busy getting rich, and Fritz Bauer's insistence on trying the Third Reich reads to his own colleagues as bad manners. A letter arrives from Argentina: a man there believes his daughter is seeing Adolph Eichmann's son. Bauer cannot hand that to the judiciary around him, staffed as it still is by men with pasts, so he carries it to Mossad in Jerusalem, an act that makes him in law a traitor. Lars Kraume builds it as a mystery whose threat is domestic rather than distant: not the fugitive abroad but the office down the hall, the colleague whose war nobody discusses. Seen from that desk, the economic miracle is mostly a very good reason for everyone to look away.

Vincent's mother dies, and his father, who holds public office, arranges for him to be admitted to a clinic. Vincent has Tourette's syndrome; the syndrome is audible; a politician's household prefers its difficulties quiet. Inside, the room comes with Alexander, whose compulsions run on their own strict schedule, and the tour of the corridors comes from Marie, anorexic, who has been there long enough to give it. Ralf Huettner films the three of them at close quarters, and the subject turns out to be custody rather than diagnosis: who decided each of them belonged here, and on whose behalf. Ninety-six minutes leaves no room for case histories, which is a mercy. What remains is three young people in a building where the doors are opened by other people, and the ordinary business of finding one another tolerable.

A sportswriter and a fashion designer marry, and then discover how little of the day they can spend in the same room. His deadline and her fitting want the same hours; his friends and hers would not choose each other; and each keeps turning up evidence of the other's earlier life. Vincente Minnelli stages the trouble domestically, in rooms where the furniture and the colour carry a share of the argument, and the comedy comes from two people who are both entirely reasonable and entirely immovable. A hundred and eighteen minutes is generous for this kind of picture, and the length goes into the slow discovery that affection and compatibility are separate accounts. The Academy gave its original-screenplay award to the result, which suits a film whose best jokes are structural rather than verbal.

Lolita has a voice worth training and a father whose attention has never once been available for it. Étienne is a literary star, surrounded by people who need something from him and who have learned the going rate for flattery; his daughter is twenty, unhappy in her body, and last in the queue. Agnès Jaoui, who wrote and directed it, sets everyone in a milieu where compliments are transactions, and nobody can accept one without first working out what it was for. Lolita's suspicion that her singing teacher cares mainly about access to Étienne is not paranoia but accurate reading. The film stays patient with the small operators, the second wife among them, the ones whose standing is borrowed and who know it, and at a hundred and ten minutes the discomfort has time to become recognizable.

A samurai leaves home because the stipend from his small clan will not feed his children. That admission, that the work is a job and the pay is short, is what Kanichiro Yoshimura carries into the city, where men of his rank are not expected to mention money. Yojiro Takita takes a hundred and thirty-seven minutes over it, and the length goes into ordinary registers rather than duels: what a wife is told, how a provincial accent lands in a room of professionals. His family stays behind, and everything Yoshimura does afterward is measured against a house he is not in. Filed as action and history, the film runs on arithmetic. It was named picture of the year by the Japan Academy Film Prize; the sword here is a trade, and the trade has a household behind it.

A hungry man is paid to vote, repeatedly, and turns out to have a gift for it. Preston Sturges builds the picture out of that promotion and the ones that follow: a Depression drifter, a city machine that needs willing hands, and a boss who decides his best asset would look convincing running as a reformer. The catch is domestic. Candidates are expected to have wives, so a marriage is arranged for the ballot rather than the house, and that is where an eighty-two-minute comedy keeps its real trouble. Sturges wrote it and the script took the Academy Award, though what stays is less the wit than the flatness of the assumptions: that graft is a career with rungs, that public virtue is a costume kept at the office, that the men running the city hide very little from each other.

The river is up, the bridge is out, and a country inn fills with people who would not otherwise share a room. Takashi Koizumi keeps nearly everything inside that building: travellers with unequal amounts of money and standing, the same corridors, the same meals, days with no shape because nobody can leave. Rain is the entire engine, which is a severe way to build a film and an efficient one, since pressure rises simply because the water does not fall. Ninety-one minutes, and the tension is social throughout: who eats first, who apologises, who was courteous before the flood and stays courteous during it. Confinement makes small politenesses expensive, and the film is precise about what they cost. Nobody at the inn chose the company.

In 1983 a German magazine published sixty volumes of Hitler's diaries and had about two weeks before the whole thing came apart. Helmut Dietl's farce starts on the forger's side: Fritz Knobel makes a living faking Nazi memorabilia, and the diaries begin as one more commission. Then a journalist smells the money in them, the orders multiply, and Knobel finds himself writing at length in another man's voice and picking up the habits that go with it. The satire lands on the buyers rather than the fake. A country that could be sold sixty volumes of its worst decade, and wanted to buy, is the actual subject, and Dietl keeps the tone light enough that the discomfort has somewhere to go. The real people are barely disguised, which in 1992 was its own kind of nerve.

Madame Tang's business is arranging what officials and developers cannot say to each other directly. She runs it from a house of women, where hospitality and leverage are the same gesture. Yang Ya-che shoots this as a thriller in which almost nothing is done by the person who wants it done, and the cruelty is procedural: a phrase, an introduction, a name left off a list. One arrangement fails, a household close to the Tangs is destroyed, and the question stops being who acted and becomes whose interest was served. The charge comes from the family itself, where the manners that manage ministers are turned inward. The Golden Horse Award for best feature went to it; the lacquered surfaces are the least trustworthy thing in it.

A theatre company calls a meeting about one of its own, and the deciding takes most of the film. Anjali is the group's only actress; after a party, a man in the troupe commits a crime against her; the others convene to arrive at a consensus. Anand Ekarshi builds the hours that follow out of talk: proposals, abstentions, an old friendship invoked at a useful moment, a career weighed against a colleague's word. The method is to let everyone sound reasonable, which is how a group protects itself while believing it is being fair. A hundred and thirty-nine minutes is not padding here; it is the length of an argument that keeps restarting, and India's National Film Award for best feature followed. The hardest thing in it is the arithmetic of who can afford to believe her.

Xiu Xiu is a teenager when the state sends her to the far edge of Sichuan to work with her hands. The year is 1975, the assignment is manual labour, and the term is not specified. A year on she agrees to go further out still, to learn horse herding from Lao Jin, a Tibetan horseman whose tent is the only address for a long way in any direction. Joan Chen, directing, puts the weight on distance as a practical fact: how far the nearest official is, what a teenager's ordinary vanity looks like in a place with no use for it. It carries the Golden Horse Award for best feature. Ninety-nine minutes, much of it spent waiting, for word, for transport, for someone at a desk to remember a name on a list.

The act is six men, five singers and a pianist, and the film gives itself exactly seven years of them. It begins in 1927, when they first meet, and runs to 1934. Joseph Vilsmaier spends the interval on the working life of a popular group: auditions, arrangements, tours, contracts, the small rivalries that arrive with sudden bookings. Three of the six are Jewish, and the years covered are precisely the ones in which that stops being a private detail. The cinematography took a European Film Award, and the reason is visible in the light, warm and plush, a Germany rendered as somewhere worth staying. A hundred and twenty-six minutes leaves room to actually hear the arrangements, and hearing them matters: what these six made was intricate, cheerful and entirely of its moment.

The work is bathing, lifting, feeding, and doing all of it again the next day, and David is unusually good at it. He nurses the terminally ill, learns their histories and their preferences, and stays past the hours he is paid for. The patients change; the routine does not. Michel Franco withholds the rest of him. Away from the bedsides, David's life is conducted with far less competence and almost no company, and the film offers no tidy account of the difference. Ninety-three minutes is brief for a drama about dying, and the brevity keeps the register clinical rather than consoling: tasks, transfers, medication times, the etiquette of being paid to be close to a stranger. Care, done this well and at this length, turns out to be a place a person can hide.
